lesson.title: ü, ö, ä — Mouth Positions
lesson.subtitle: Pronunciation clinic with minimal pairs — schon/schön, Bruder/Brüder

hook.title: Three Vowels English Skipped
hook.content: German has three front-rounded vowels English never kept: ü, ö, ä. The trick is mechanical, not magical: say the English vowel (e, o, a) and ROUND YOUR LIPS at the same time — say 'ee' with 'oo'-lips and you have ü. The minimal pairs prove the difference is meaning-level: schon (already) vs schön (beautiful) differ by one mouth position. Bruder (brother) vs Brüder (brothers) differ by umlaut — the plural dots you know from the i-mutation lesson are also a SOUND change. English once had these sounds (it kept them in French loanwords like 'curve' and 'rare'); German kept them native.

footnotes.title: The Three Positions
footnotes.content: ü = say 'ee' with rounded lips (über — the V→B preposition!). ö = say 'ay' with rounded lips (schön, zwölf). ä = say 'eh' with slightly laxer tongue (Männer, Mädchen). ä is the easiest — many dialects merge it with plain e; ü and ö are the real work.

pattern.title: Minimal Pair Drills
pattern.content: Pair one: schon (already — Schon gut! 'already fine') vs schön (beautiful — Schön! 'nice!'). Pair two: Bruder (brother) vs Brüder (brothers) — the umlaut you learned as spelling is this sound. Pair three: morgen (morning) vs Mörder (murderer — grim but unforgettable). Pair four: zwölf (twelve) — the ö inside the number you already count. Pair five: über (over) vs unter? — unter has none, but öl (oil) does. Drill the pairs aloud: the vowels are mouth POSITIONS, and your mouth can learn a position in an afternoon.
pattern.linguist_note: Front-rounded vowels are the Germanic umlaut made audible: historical i pulled the vowel forward AND English/German rounded what remained differently. English kept the roundness only in French loans (curve, urgent, purse) — the sounds exist in your mouth already, just unassigned.

exercises.prompt: Minimal pair: 'Das ist schön!' — what does the ö change from 'schon'?
exercises.meaning: The ü/ö minimal pair with real meaning stakes
exercises.explanation: One mouth position separates 'already' from 'beautiful' — say 'ay' with rounded lips for the ö.

exercises.prompt: How do you make the ü sound?
options: There is no ü in German
Say 'ee' while rounding your lips like for 'oo'
exercises.target_answer: Say 'ee' while rounding your lips like for 'oo'
exercises.explanation: Front tongue + rounded lips = ü. über, Tür, dünn — the vowel you have been reading all trail. Say the pair you meet in every shop: die Tüte, das Öl — the first held long, the second rounded long.

the PLURAL of Mann — the men-fossil

exercises.target_answer: the PLURAL of Bruder — umlaut as sound, twelve — the tw→zw number, the PLURAL of Mann — the men-fossil, beautiful — the minimal-pair star
exercises.explanation: The dots are not decoration — they are the vowel-pull you learned in the plurals lesson, made audible.

exercises.prompt: Which word does NOT contain an umlaut vowel?
exercises.explanation: über (ü), zwölf (ö), Mädchen (ä) — but unter is the plain twin of under, no dots. Same for Herr, and for the trap-deck nouns riding along on this page: die Fabrik, das Gymnasium, die Rente, der Dom, die Art, die Kaution, eventuell.

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'My brother is twelve' (with the ü-recipe in my...)
exercises.meaning: Mein Bruder ist zwölf = My brother is twelve

vocab_hints.note: mein ↔ mine — the possessive twin from the Article Grid

exercises.explanation: Three old friends, one sentence — and zwölf wears the ö you just learned to round.

summary.outcome: Produce ü, ö, ä and distinguish the minimal pairs schon/schön, Bruder/Brüder.
summary.takeaway: ü = 'ee' with round lips, ö = 'ay' with round lips, ä = lax 'eh' — the umlaut dots are sounds, not decorations.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the Ablaut Hall of Fame — a guided tour of all seven strong verb classes.

bruder.etymology_derivation: Medial th shifted to d; unstressed -er vocalizes to [ɐ].

morgen.etymology_derivation: Cognate with English morrow (hence to-morrow) and morn — both descend from the Germanic root for "morning". [wiktionary]

zwölf.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *twalif — 'two left over', the exact tw → zw twin of twelve. [wiktionary]

schön.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *skauniz — the twin of archaic English sheen 'beautiful'. [wiktionary]

öl.context_phrase: Ich brate das Ei in Öl.
öl.context_translation: I fry the egg in oil.
öl.etymology_derivation: From West Germanic oli, meaning olive oil, ultimately from Latin oleum; English oil descends from the same early Latin loan into Old English. [wiktionary]

tüte.etymology_derivation: From Low German tute, a conical bag — the page lists English tote as the cognate: the bag you tote things in. [wiktionary]

herr.context_translation: The gentleman is called Mr. Müller.
herr.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *hairaz 'grey' — the grey-haired one, cognate with English hoar. [wiktionary]

fabrik.etymology_derivation: Both from Latin fabrica — true cognates, drifted senses. Trap: die Fabrik = FACTORY. (Fabric: der Stoff.) [wiktionary]

gymnasium.etymology_derivation: Both from the Greek wrestling-ground — true cognates, drifted senses. Trap: das Gymnasium = ACADEMIC HIGH SCHOOL. (Gym: die Turnhalle.) [wiktionary]

rente.etymology_derivation: Both from Latin rendere — true cognates, drifted senses. Trap: die Rente = PENSION. (Apartment rent: die Miete.) [wiktionary]

dom.etymology_derivation: Both from Latin domus (church-house) — true cognates, drifted senses. Trap: der Dom = CATHEDRAL. (Dome: die Kuppel.) [wiktionary]

art.context_phrase: Diese Art von Buch ist gut.
art.context_translation: This kind of book is good.
art.etymology_derivation: Both from Latin ars/artis — true cognates, drifted senses. Trap: die Art = KIND/TYPE. (Fine art: die Kunst.) [wiktionary]

kaution.etymology_derivation: Both from Latin cautio — true cognates, drifted senses. Trap: die Kaution = SECURITY DEPOSIT. (Caution: die Vorsicht.) [wiktionary]

eventuell.etymology_derivation: Both from Latin eventus — true cognates, drifted senses. Trap: eventuell = POSSIBLY. (Eventually: schließlich/am Ende.) [wiktionary]

abendbrot.context_phrase: Um sechs essen wir das Abendbrot.
abendbrot.etymology_derivation: Abend + Brot, literally evening bread — the German supper; Abend is the twin of archaic English even and Brot the twin of bread. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
